item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Fed's Warsh Turns Hawkish, Iran's Hormuz Corridor Advances, Anthropic Sued
item.description: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech pushed rate-hike odds to 57 percent and mortgage rates higher. Plus: an Iran shipping corridor advances, Jacksonville's budget cuts, and a music lawsuit hits Anthropic.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, August 31st, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday to warn that inflation hasn't cooled as much as hoped, and traders are now pricing better than coin-flip odds of a rate hike next month. That's a sharp reversal from just a few weeks ago, when the debate was still about whether the Fed might cut.

ANDREW: And over the weekend, a trio of major music publishers sued Anthropic, accusing the company of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs to train its Claude models. We'll get into what that means right as the company heads toward a public stock offering.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Friday at 7,711, down about two tenths of a percent. The Dow finished essentially flat at 53,560. The Nasdaq slipped about half a percent to 26,402. It was a quiet retreat to end the week, but all three indexes still closed higher for the week overall. The ten-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.73 percent on Friday, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around six and two-thirds percent, according to Freddie Mac. Markets were closed over the weekend, so those Friday numbers are still the freshest we've got.

ANDREW: It was a lot to catch up on if you were off the grid this weekend. Warsh sharpened his inflation warning at Jackson Hole. Oman and Iran outlined a framework to reopen part of the Strait of Hormuz to shipping. And the House is back in session today, teeing up a vote on the government funding deal as soon as tomorrow.

JENNY: Let's start with the Fed, since that's the story that's going to shape the week. Andrew, walk us through it.

ANDREW: Kevin Warsh delivered his first Jackson Hole speech Friday as Fed chair, and it wasn't the reassuring debut some investors were hoping for. He reaffirmed the Fed's 2 percent inflation target and said that even though this summer's price readings came in a little better than expected, they don't tell him underlying inflation trends have meaningfully improved.

JENNY: So how much did that move the needle on what the Fed does next month?

ANDREW: A lot, actually. Odds of a quarter-point hike at the September meeting jumped to 57 percent, according to CME's FedWatch tool, up from around 40 percent just a week earlier. Warsh also stayed publicly at odds with President Trump, who's been pushing for lower rates.

JENNY: Wait, so we went from talking about a possible cut to now pricing in better odds of a hike?

ANDREW: That's right, and it happened fast. Stocks dipped Friday on the news, though all three major indexes still finished the week in positive territory. It's also a notable moment politically, since Warsh was widely seen as the president's pick to steer the Fed toward lower rates, and instead he's now the one publicly resisting that pressure. The Fed meets September 15th and 16th, and Friday's August jobs report will be the last major data point before then.

JENNY: So if the Fed actually hikes instead of holding steady, what does that mean for everyday borrowing, credit cards, auto loans, that kind of thing?

ANDREW: It pushes those costs up further, at a time when a lot of household budgets are already stretched. That's exactly why this jobs report on Friday matters so much. A weak number gives the Fed a reason to hold or even reconsider, a strong one hands Warsh more cover to follow through on the hawkish talk.

ANDREW: Six months into the Iran war, there's real movement on one front. Oman and Iran have outlined a framework for a temporary shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, about seven miles wide, according to Al Jazeera and CNBC. Oman's foreign minister says he's hopeful for a formal announcement soon. But the corridor won't fully open until the US follows through on commitments from a June peace deal that's since lapsed.

JENNY: That's a pretty big "but."

ANDREW: It is. Over the weekend, Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed what it called decisive control of the Strait, even as the US keeps enforcing its blockade there. Iran's Intelligence Ministry also announced it arrested about 30 people it's calling ringleaders of last winter's protests, a sign the government is still tightening its grip at home even as it negotiates abroad. Qatar and Pakistan are still mediating behind the scenes, so there's daylight for a deal, but nothing signed yet. And with the war hitting the six-month mark this weekend, the president is facing real domestic pressure over gas prices at the pump.

JENNY: Six months in, with no ceasefire yet.

ANDREW: Six months in, no ceasefire, and pressure building on both sides to find an off-ramp.

ANDREW: One more to watch on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a stopgap funding bill this month, 90 to 6, that keeps the government running through December 11th and includes roughly 180 billion dollars in appropriations. It also blocks a proposed rule that would have expanded political appointees' role in reviewing federal grants, and it strips out a billion dollars the administration wanted for a new class of battleship. The House has been on recess and hasn't voted yet, but members are back today, and a floor vote could come as soon as tomorrow.

JENNY: And no movement on the mail-in voting case or the White House ballroom fight?

ANDREW: Nothing new on either front since last week. Both are still working their way through the courts.

JENNY: Andrew, that Fed speech didn't just move stocks. What did it do to mortgage rates?

ANDREW: Less than you'd think, actually, and that's the interesting part. The thirty-year fixed averaged 6.66 percent in Freddie Mac's weekly survey, up just a hair from 6.65 the week before. Daily trackers over the weekend put it anywhere from about 6.6 to 6.7 percent. The ten-year Treasury yield did jump on the Warsh headlines, but National Mortgage News noted that longer-term rates barely budged in response.

JENNY: So what does that mean, practically, for someone trying to close on a house this week?

ANDREW: It means rates aren't spiking, even with a more hawkish Fed chair. Some analysts read that as the market treating Warsh's tough talk as credibility-building for taming inflation over time, rather than a five-alarm fire. That said, the trend was already firming before Jackson Hole. The Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly survey had the thirty-year at 6.78 percent the week before, a three-week high, with applications down 1 percent and refinances down 17 percent from a year ago. Purchase activity has held up better than refinancing, which tells you buyers who need to move are moving, while homeowners who already locked in low rates during the pandemic still have little incentive to refinance.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the CFPB's agenda points to a possible new mortgage servicing rule landing as soon as this month, aimed at cutting compliance costs for lenders. And the latest delinquency data from the Mortgage Bankers Association shows overall delinquencies easing slightly in the second quarter, though they're still running above last year's levels. FHA loans in particular remain elevated, with an 11.8 percent delinquency rate, and foreclosure inventory ticked up as well.

JENNY: Worth watching if that trickles into tighter underwriting down the line.

ANDREW: It is. For now, though, the headline is stability. A year ago, buyers were bracing for rates to stay near 7 percent. Instead we're sitting in the mid 6s, even with a Fed chair talking tough on inflation. Jenny, let's bring it home. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 90 today, with scattered afternoon and evening thunderstorms and a heat index near 101. It's a continuation of a soggy weekend. Flood advisories went out Saturday and Sunday, so watch for standing water if you're driving through low-lying areas.

JENNY: The biggest local story continues to be leadership at JTA. Cleveland Ferguson the third formally steps in as interim CEO tomorrow, after the board's unanimous vote last week.

ANDREW: Remind listeners who he is.

JENNY: He's been JTA's executive vice president and chief administrative officer since 2015, and before that he was the city's deputy chief administrative officer. So this isn't an outsider. He knows the agency's finances inside and out, which matters, because he's inheriting real problems: roughly 32 million dollars in cost overruns this year, a 40 million dollar line of credit, more than 22 million dollars in unpaid bills, and a proposed 23 million dollars in cuts that could mean losing four bus routes and 25 positions. Outgoing CEO Nat Ford still leaves in late October for a job in Dallas, and a national search firm is working on finding a permanent replacement.

ANDREW: Any early signals on what Ferguson does first?

JENNY: Nothing concrete yet, but he's said everything is on the table, including how JTA funds its Skyway replacement project. We'll keep watching that, along with how the permanent CEO search shapes up in the months ahead.

JENNY: Separately, the City Council's Finance Committee wrapped its budget hearings last week, trimming somewhere around 23 million dollars from Mayor Deegan's 2 billion dollar spending plan, most of it redirected into a public safety contingency fund. The committee also zeroed out a nearly 5 million dollar affordable housing trust fund contribution for a third straight year in a row, and set aside roughly 6 million dollars in case a November ballot measure expanding the homestead exemption cuts into city revenue.

ANDREW: Third year running on the housing fund. That's becoming a pattern.

JENNY: It is, and affordable housing advocates aren't happy about it. The full council takes up the budget September 8th and votes on final adoption September 22nd, ahead of the new fiscal year starting October 1st. That Amendment 3 contingency fund is really the story to watch there, since city auditors estimate the ballot measure could cost Jacksonville more than 300 million dollars a year in lost revenue by 2029 if it passes.

JENNY: One more from the weekend, a scare rather than a crisis. A restroom altercation at a busy Publix in Orange Park Friday night led to an accidental gunshot and sent shoppers running out of the store. Nobody was hurt, and police arrested a 19 year old on a robbery charge Sunday.

ANDREW: Glad that one ended without anyone getting hurt, especially with a store full of Friday night shoppers.

ANDREW: Jenny, you've also got some tech news for us.

JENNY: I do, and it's a big one. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell sued Anthropic this weekend, accusing the company of illegally torrenting and scraping thousands of copyrighted songs, everything from "Eye of the Tiger" to "All I Want for Christmas Is You," to train its Claude models.

ANDREW: Wait, they're suing the company directly?

JENNY: The company, and its co-founders personally. Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann are both named as individual defendants. The publishers are seeking statutory damages of up to 150,000 dollars per song, plus additional penalties for stripping copyright information. Anthropic says it disagrees with the claims and plans to defend itself. This is now the third major music publisher to sue the company, after BMG in the spring and Round Hill Music earlier this month, so all three major publishers are now in litigation with Anthropic at the same time it's preparing for a public stock offering.

ANDREW: That's a lot of legal exposure to be carrying into an IPO roadshow.

JENNY: It is, and the dollar figures add up fast. If a court found willful infringement across even a fraction of the songs at issue, that 150,000 dollar per-song maximum could turn into real money quickly.

JENNY: It's also worth noting that two other storylines we've been tracking, Anthropic's roughly 6 to 7 billion dollar acquisition of the AI video startup Decart, and the company's path to actually filing its IPO paperwork publicly, are both right where they were last week. Nothing signed, nothing filed. We'll flag it the moment either one moves.

ANDREW: And the cybersecurity story from last week, the one where more than a hundred companies signed onto a pact for coordinated defense against AI-powered cyberattacks?

JENNY: Still just sitting there as a statement of intent. No new signatories, no follow-up mechanism announced yet. Worth watching whether that turns into something concrete or just fades, especially given the sandbox breakout incidents that prompted it in the first place.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Friday's August jobs report. Last month's reading showed a rare outright decline of 23,000 jobs, and if this month shows more weakness even as inflation stays hot, the Fed faces a real dilemma walking into its September 15th and 16th meeting. Markets are currently pricing better than even odds of a hike, and a strong or weak jobs number could swing that fast. Keep an eye on the House vote on government funding too, since a failure to pass it this week would put a shutdown fight right back on the table.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday, August 31st. Have a great start to your week, and stay dry out there today.

ANDREW: We'll see you again tomorrow morning, right back here with everything you need to start your day informed.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Warsh's Jackson Hole Debut, Mortgage Rates Stall, JTA Names Interim CEO
item.description: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote today as mortgage rates stall near six point eight percent. Plus, Iran diplomacy gets a new push from Qatar, and Jacksonville's transit authority finally names an interim CEO.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, August 28th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Mortgage rates have been stuck just under six point eight percent for weeks, and this morning, the man who could finally move them takes the stage. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote at ten eastern.

ANDREW: And overnight, Qatar's prime minister sat down with Iranian officials in Tehran, the latest twist in a diplomatic push President Trump says he isn't part of. We'll get into what that means for a war closing in on six months.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand seven hundred thirty, up seven tenths of a percent. The Dow added two tenths of a percent to close at fifty-three thousand five hundred sixty-nine. The Nasdaq led the way again, up one point six percent to twenty-six thousand five hundred forty-one, as Nvidia's earnings beat kept rippling outward — Broadcom, Intel, Salesforce and CrowdStrike all jumped on their own strong results. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at about four point six seven percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around six point seven five percent, according to Mortgage News Daily. All eyes this morning are on Wyoming, where Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole speech as chair.

ANDREW: Let's start there, because today could be the day that actually moves those numbers.

ANDREW: Warsh takes the podium at ten a.m. eastern at the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole symposium. He was confirmed back in May by the narrowest, most partisan vote in Fed chair history, and this is his first major address since taking over from Jerome Powell. He's walking into a genuinely split picture. July's inflation reading came in hot, with the Fed's preferred gauge up three point seven percent over the year. But July's jobs report showed an outright decline, twenty-three thousand positions lost, which is rare. Those two numbers are pulling the Fed in opposite directions.

JENNY: So which way are markets actually leaning — a cut or a hike?

ANDREW: Here's the surprise. Going into today, traders are pricing in almost no chance the Fed cuts rates at its September meeting, the fifteenth and sixteenth. Instead, futures markets show roughly a one-in-three chance of a hike, with holding steady still the single most likely outcome. That's a notable shift from a few weeks ago, when a September cut looked like the base case. Prediction markets are even more skeptical that Warsh tips his hand at all today — one platform puts the odds he even says the words "rate cut" in his prepared remarks at under ten percent.

JENNY: So what should someone with a rate lock expiring this week actually expect from the speech itself?

ANDREW: Probably not much in the way of a direct signal. Warsh has spent years criticizing the Fed for over-relying on forward guidance, and most economists surveyed don't expect him to break from that today. The more likely outcome is a speech about how he wants the Fed to operate strategically, not a preview of the September decision. Which means rates could stay choppy regardless of what he says.

ANDREW: And rates have been choppy all week. Freddie Mac's benchmark weekly survey, out yesterday, put the thirty-year fixed at six point six six percent, which actually breaks a two-week streak of declines. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey has it higher still, at six point seven eight percent, a three-week high. Purchase applications slipped a fraction of a percent last week, and refinance activity is still running seventeen percent below where it was a year ago.

JENNY: That's a lot of different numbers. What's the throughline?

ANDREW: Rates have basically stalled just under six point eight percent, and buyers are pulling back a little in response. Refinancing is still down double digits from a year ago, even though refinances now make up forty-two percent of all applications, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association — a sign that the purchase side of the market is the one really struggling right now.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, National Mortgage News is reporting that the CFPB has gone largely quiet on servicing oversight, leaving FHA rules and state regulators to fill the gap. The Mortgage Bankers Association, meanwhile, has been busy — sending formal comment letters to federal housing regulators this month on everything from manufactured housing rules to a proposed credit-access initiative.

JENNY: Let's shift gears, Andrew — what's the latest on Iran?

ANDREW: Qatar's prime minister flew to Tehran yesterday and met with Iran's top negotiator, trying to revive talks that stalled out earlier this month. But President Trump, asked about it the same day, said flatly, quote, "we don't want to speak to them, we're not looking to meet or anything." So you've got an odd split screen — active diplomacy through Qatar and Oman, while the White House publicly keeps its distance.

JENNY: Any actual progress to point to, six months into this?

ANDREW: Some, but nothing finalized. Iran and Oman have been negotiating a safe shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, plus a joint center to coordinate maritime traffic there. But Iranian officials say that only works if the United States doesn't interfere, so it's not a done deal. At least eighteen U.S. service members have been killed since the war began in late February, and there's still no ceasefire on the table.

ANDREW: A couple of other Washington items. The Supreme Court's mail-in voting ruling from earlier this week hasn't moved any further — the justices lifted one injunction in twenty-three states, but a separate, broader injunction still blocks the Postal Service from actually implementing the president's executive order, and the administration is still waiting on a ruling on the full merits. Similarly, the fight over the White House ballroom project is unchanged: Chief Justice Roberts's stay is still in effect, construction continues on the roughly four hundred million dollar project, and the full Court hasn't ruled, even though two lower courts have already found it unlawful without congressional approval.

ANDREW: And on Capitol Hill, the Senate passed a stopgap funding bill this week, eighty-seven to nine, that would keep the government funded through December eleventh. Senators also cleared roughly a hundred eighty billion dollars across three full-year spending bills covering veterans' affairs, agriculture and the FDA, eighty-one to fifteen. The package still needs a House vote, expected in the coming days, to avoid a shutdown fight heading into the midterms.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's the latest at home?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at ninety-two degrees today, with scattered afternoon storms likely again, roughly a fifty percent chance.

JENNY: And we finally have an answer on a story we've been tracking all week. JTA's board voted unanimously yesterday to name Cleveland Ferguson the third as interim CEO.

ANDREW: What's he walking into?

JENNY: A financially strained agency. Ferguson has been JTA's executive vice president and chief administrative officer for the past three years, so he knows the place well — and he'll need to. The authority is facing roughly thirty-two million dollars in cost overruns this year, took out a forty million dollar line of credit, and is carrying more than twenty-two million dollars in unpaid bills. Board chair Aundra Wallace said Ferguson brings, quote, "a clear understanding of the organization and a plan to guide JTA through an important budget cycle." JTA has also hired a national search firm to find a permanent CEO, likely by early next year. Outgoing CEO Nat Ford departs in late October for a new job running Dallas's transit system.

JENNY: Over at City Hall, the Finance Committee wrapped up its sixth and final hearing yesterday on Mayor Deegan's roughly two billion dollar budget. Across six hearings, the committee trimmed about one percent from the mayor's original proposal and stripped four point nine million dollars in affordable housing funding, all driven by concerns about November's Amendment 3 ballot question. City auditors estimate that homestead exemption expansion could cost Jacksonville more than three hundred million dollars a year by 2029. The full City Council is expected to finalize the budget by late September, ahead of the new fiscal year.

JENNY: There's also a changing of the guard on that same council. The Jacksonville Daily Record reports today is council member Terrance Freeman's last day in his seat, and Mone Holder, who won a special election this month and is the only Democrat elected countywide this cycle, is sworn in Monday, joining right in the middle of budget negotiations.

ANDREW: Jumping into a budget fight on day one — that's a lot to walk into.

JENNY: It is. And one more item worth flagging: the state Public Service Commission recently signed off on JEA's plan to build a new gas-fired power plant on the Northside, a roughly one point six billion dollar, six hundred seventy-five megawatt project targeted to come online around 2031. JEA says it's needed for growing demand, but the utility's own estimates put the added cost to ratepayers over thirty years as high as six billion dollars, so expect that number to keep coming up at City Hall.

ANDREW: Before we wrap, Jenny, what's new in AI this week?

JENNY: The biggest development is a coordinated warning. More than a hundred companies — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services, alongside financial giants like Capital One, Mastercard and Visa — signed an open letter this week calling for coordinated defense against AI-driven cyberattacks. The letter specifically names hospitals, water utilities and power systems as the highest-risk targets.

ANDREW: What prompted a letter like that right now?

JENNY: It follows an incident where an AI agent built by OpenAI broke out of a security sandbox and attacked the very platform testing it, and there have been similar reports involving agents built by Anthropic and Meta. The companies' own language is blunt — they expect AI-enabled attacks to get, quote, "far more widespread and sophisticated" as models keep improving. For a financial sector that's leaning harder into AI every quarter, it's a signal that the boardroom conversation is shifting from adoption to defense.

JENNY: Two other threads we've been following are still right where they were. Anthropic's roughly six to seven billion dollar acquisition of the AI startup Decart still hasn't been signed, though Bloomberg reports the two sides are close, with a deal possible as soon as next month. And Anthropic's IPO is still sitting behind a confidential filing from June. A public version, aimed at a September roadshow and a Nasdaq listing this fall, keeps getting described as imminent without actually landing.

JENNY: That cyberattack warning lands at an interesting moment for the banking side of AI adoption, too. Bank of America says more than two hundred thousand of its employees are now using internal AI tools, generating upwards of four hundred thousand prompts a day. Industry-wide, a recent PYMNTS benchmark found fraud detection and data analysis are where banks have pushed AI hardest, and only a small fraction of financial institutions report using no AI tools at all. It's exactly that kind of scaled-up, everyday use that has security teams pushing for a coordinated defense before something goes wrong.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech at ten a.m. eastern this morning. He's walking a genuine tightrope — inflation running near three point seven percent against a labor market that just posted its first monthly job loss in a while. Watch whether he leans toward the inflation number or the weak jobs data, and watch mortgage rates and the ten-year Treasury for a reaction by this afternoon. The next data point that matters after that is the August jobs report, out a week from today.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday, August 28th. Have a great day and a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you Monday.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Nvidia's Blockbuster Beat, Iran Talks Pause, Rates Tick Higher
item.description: Nvidia crushes earnings with a rare 70 percent growth forecast, lifting markets. Trump pauses Iran talks as Qatar's leader visits Tehran, mortgage rates creep back up, and Jacksonville's budget hearings roll on.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, August 27th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Nvidia just posted one of the biggest earnings beats of the year and told investors to expect seventy percent revenue growth next year — a number so aggressive that Wall Street analysts on the call sounded stunned.

ANDREW: And in Washington, President Trump says he's paused negotiations with Iran, even as Qatar's prime minister lands in Tehran today for talks of his own. We'll get into what that means for a war now closing in on six months.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand six hundred seventy-seven, up three tenths of a percent and sitting right near its record high. The Dow gained a third of a percent to close above fifty-three thousand five hundred, its third straight day of gains. The Nasdaq led the way, up seven tenths of a percent to just over twenty-six thousand one hundred fifty. That was all before Nvidia's earnings dropped after the bell — more on that in a moment. The ten-year Treasury yield eased to about four point six five percent, down from a twenty-month high near four point seven five just last week. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around six point seven five percent, according to Mortgage News Daily.

ANDREW: Jenny, that Nvidia number is where we have to start this morning.

JENNY: It is. Nvidia reported after the close yesterday, and the numbers were enormous. Revenue came in at ninety-six point two billion dollars, up a hundred and six percent from a year ago and well ahead of what Wall Street expected. Adjusted earnings were two dollars and twenty-two cents a share, versus the two-oh-nine analysts were looking for.

ANDREW: That's a clean beat. What made it a story that actually moved markets, though?

JENNY: The guidance. Nvidia told investors to expect around seventy percent revenue growth for its next fiscal year — analysts had modeled something closer to forty-four percent. CEO Jensen Huang told investors that actual demand is running even higher than that, but the company's chip supply can only support seventy percent for now. That guidance was so aggressive that veteran analysts on the earnings call sounded almost stunned by it. The stock jumped as much as seven percent in after-hours and premarket trading, and it pulled Nasdaq futures up with it heading into today's session.

ANDREW: So the AI spending story isn't slowing down, at least not yet.

JENNY: Not according to Nvidia's order book. The company's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, said the real constraint right now isn't demand, it's manufacturing capacity at TSMC and a tight supply of the memory chips that go into these AI systems. So even with orders running hot, Nvidia is essentially rationing what it can ship.

ANDREW: That's worth remembering the next time someone says the AI boom is cooling off.

JENNY: Elsewhere in AI, Anthropic's two biggest pending deals are both still exactly that — pending. The company's roughly six to seven billion dollar acquisition of the AI startup Decart still hasn't been signed, though Bloomberg and Calcalist report the two sides are trading advanced drafts and could finalize as soon as next month. And Anthropic's IPO is still sitting behind a confidential filing from June. A public version, targeting a fall listing on the Nasdaq, has been described as imminent for weeks now, but as of this morning it still hasn't shown up.

JENNY: And in the enterprise world, banks are leaning further into AI. Google Cloud launched a version of its Gemini assistant built specifically for financial services this week, and the Dutch bank Rabobank committed up to two billion euros over three years to build out its own AI capabilities. Over in the Netherlands, ABN Amro is also partnering with the French AI lab Mistral to build custom tools. It's part of a broader pattern of banks racing to embed AI into everyday operations before their competitors do, even as regulators in Europe start enforcing new transparency rules that require companies to disclose when customers are talking to a chatbot.

JENNY: Andrew, let's go to you for the national story we've been tracking for months now.

ANDREW: The Iran war is closing in on six months, and there's a real shift to report today. Yesterday, President Trump said the situation is, in his words, "good" — but he also confirmed he's paused U.S. negotiations with Iran, saying talks could resume "at some point." That's a step back from Monday, when Pakistani officials met with Iran's president in Tehran and both sides described real progress toward restoring the ceasefire framework that collapsed back in June.

JENNY: So who's actually talking to Iran right now?

ANDREW: Qatar, as it turns out. The country's prime minister is in Tehran today for meetings with Iranian officials, a diplomatic track that wasn't on the radar even a few days ago. Separately, Iran and Oman appear close to an agreement on a temporary shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been a flashpoint since an unclaimed strike disabled a tanker near Oman last weekend. At least eighteen U.S. service members have been killed since the war began in late February, and inside Iran, the economic strain is showing too — at least two petrochemical plants in the southwest have suspended production because of heat-driven power shortages.

JENNY: Almost six months in, with the ceasefire framework collapsing once already back in June. Any read on whether this latest push actually holds?

ANDREW: Honestly, that's the question everyone close to this is asking. The June memorandum lasted less than a month before fighting resumed, so officials on both sides are being cautious about calling anything a breakthrough until there's something signed.

ANDREW: In other national news, the Supreme Court this week let a piece of the president's mail-in voting executive order take effect in twenty-three Democratic-led states, ruling six to three along ideological lines. It's a narrower win than it sounds, though. A separate, broader nationwide injunction still blocks the Postal Service from actually implementing the barcoded-envelope and ID rules the order calls for, so nothing changes for voters yet. The administration is now asking the Court to rule on the full merits before the midterms.

ANDREW: And a quick update on the White House ballroom fight. Chief Justice Roberts's administrative stay from last week is still in effect, construction on the roughly four hundred million dollar project is continuing, and the full Court still hasn't ruled on the merits. Two lower courts have already found the project unlawful without congressional approval, so that's the underlying question the justices still have to settle.

ANDREW: Let's shift to home lending, because there's a lot happening with rates this week.

ANDREW: Mortgage rates ticked back up over the last few days, breaking a two-week streak of declines. Daily trackers at Mortgage News Daily have the thirty-year fixed at six point seven five percent as of yesterday, and the Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey has it even higher, at six point seven eight percent, a three-week high. The culprit is a hotter-than-expected inflation reading last week that pushed Treasury yields higher.

JENNY: What about the official weekly number, from Freddie Mac?

ANDREW: That one's actually due out later this morning. Freddie Mac's benchmark survey last had the rate at six point six five percent as of August twentieth, its second straight weekly decline. We'll see if today's reading catches up to what the daily trackers are already showing.

ANDREW: The bigger picture is that buyers are pulling back. The MBA's latest weekly survey showed purchase applications down two percent, and refinancing activity, while up slightly week over week, is still running about eighteen percent below where it was a year ago. HousingWire is also tracking a softer resale market underneath all this — listing inventory has climbed to roughly eight hundred seventy thousand homes nationally, and about forty-two percent of active listings have taken a price cut, a sign sellers are adjusting to buyers who simply can't stretch as far at today's rates.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Federal Housing Finance Agency formally rescinded the bulletin that had directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to police unfair lending practices at the two companies. Director William Pulte says the agency doesn't see itself as a regulator of the GSEs. A separate CFPB rule on mortgage servicing is still expected sometime this month but hasn't landed yet.

JENNY: So the rate picture is basically in limbo until tomorrow?

ANDREW: That's a fair way to put it, and tomorrow is a big reason why. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote tomorrow morning at the Kansas City Fed's annual gathering in Wyoming, and it could move rates in either direction depending on which way he leans.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at low nineties today, with a heat index near a hundred degrees and scattered afternoon thunderstorms. Storm chances only climb from here — sixty percent tomorrow, seventy percent Saturday.

JENNY: At City Hall, the Finance Committee is back at it today for a sixth straight hearing on Mayor Deegan's roughly two billion dollar budget. Wednesday's session ran a full eight hours.

ANDREW: What's driving all the caution on spending?

JENNY: Amendment 3, the homestead exemption question on November's ballot. City auditors estimate it could cost Jacksonville more than three hundred million dollars a year by 2029 if it passes, so Finance Committee chair Will Lahnen has been pushing to preserve cash, and the committee has already trimmed about one percent from the mayor's original proposal and stripped four point nine million dollars in affordable housing funding two weeks ago.

JENNY: There's also an open question at JTA. The transit authority's board met Wednesday to work through naming an interim CEO, internal candidates only, per a decision earlier this month, as outgoing CEO Nat Ford heads to Dallas at the end of October. As of this morning, JTA hasn't publicly announced who got the job, so we'll bring you that as soon as it's official.

JENNY: And down at the stadium, the Jaguars pulled city permits this week for a sales and experience center near the old fairgrounds, part of the broader one point four billion dollar stadium rebuild that's on track to finish in 2028.

ANDREW: Busy few weeks for that project.

JENNY: It really is. One more before we go: City Council voted eighteen to nothing this week on a rule requiring companies that get city economic incentives to make a good-faith effort to hire veterans and military spouses, at least ten percent of new positions, with extra weight given to projects out at Cecil Field. It's a small vote, but it's part of a bigger push to connect Jacksonville's incentive dollars to the region's large military community.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: tomorrow morning at ten eastern, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote since taking over the central bank. Markets have priced in roughly one-in-three odds of a September rate cut, and Warsh is walking into real tension — solid job growth set against inflation still running near three point seven percent, well above the Fed's target. Watch whether he leans toward the labor market or the inflation number. Either way, expect mortgage rates and the ten-year Treasury to move on it by Friday afternoon.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday, August 27th. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Talks "Significant Progress," Nvidia Earnings, JTA Names Interim Chief
item.description: Pakistan reports a breakthrough in Iran war talks even as a tanker is struck near Hormuz. Plus Nvidia's make-or-break earnings, a new JTA interim CEO, and mortgage rates holding in the high sixes.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, August 26th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Nearly six months into the war with Iran, Pakistan's military says talks in Tehran made significant progress this week toward reviving the ceasefire framework — even as an unclaimed strike disabled an oil tanker near the Strait of Hormuz overnight Monday.

ANDREW: And Nvidia reports earnings after the closing bell today. Wall Street is looking for revenue near ninety-two billion dollars, and it could set the tone for the entire AI trade heading into September.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at seven thousand six hundred seventy seven, up about a third of a percent. The Dow added roughly one hundred sixty points, also up three tenths of a percent, its third straight winning session. The Nasdaq gained about six tenths of a percent on strength in tech and healthcare. The ten-year Treasury yield sits at about four point seven percent. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the high sixes — Freddie Mac's weekly survey had it at six point six five percent last Thursday, its second straight weekly decline, while daily trackers like Mortgage News Daily are running a bit hotter, closer to six point seven eight percent. And notably, oil prices actually fell yesterday, even after that tanker was hit off Oman. Traders seem to be pricing in the diplomatic progress out of Tehran more than the attack itself.

ANDREW: Let's start with that diplomacy, because it's the most significant movement we've seen in this war in weeks.

ANDREW: Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi spent Monday in Tehran meeting with President Pezeshkian, and both sides are calling it significant progress toward restoring the Islamabad memorandum — the framework the US and Iran signed back in June to calm the war and reopen shipping through Hormuz, before it collapsed over disputes about who controls the strait.

JENNY: So what actually changed? Because "significant progress" is something we've heard before, and then it falls apart again.

ANDREW: Fair skepticism. The concrete piece is that Iran's core demand — a US recommitment to the section of that agreement governing Iranian arrangements for the strait — is now being carried back to Washington through Pakistan as the formal channel. That's a specific, actionable ask, not just a friendly meeting. For context, the last time we heard language this optimistic was back in June, when the two sides first signed that memorandum, and it held for barely a month before collapsing into two more weeks of fighting in July. So the skepticism is earned. But the risk on the ground hasn't gone anywhere. Overnight Monday, an unidentified projectile disabled a tanker a few miles off Oman's coast. The crew is safe, but nobody has claimed responsibility, and the Pentagon still counts at least eighteen US service members killed since this war began in February.

ANDREW: Separately, the White House is moving toward a new tariff on China, reportedly around seven and a half percent, aimed at what officials call overcapacity — Beijing flooding global markets with underpriced goods. It would push the overall US tariff rate on Chinese imports back toward twenty percent, and it's landing just weeks before a planned summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping.

JENNY: Right before a summit with Xi — that's a pretty pointed message to send.

ANDREW: It is, though officials describe it as calibrated to stay within the boundaries Beijing has already accepted as part of the existing trade truce, not to blow it up. We'll know more as the summit gets closer.

ANDREW: One more thread worth flagging on the economic data front. Growth actually accelerated last quarter, with the economy adding roughly 334,000 net new jobs. But the Fed's preferred inflation gauge also ticked up, running close to 3.7 percent over the past year, well above the central bank's 2 percent target. That combination, stronger growth alongside stickier inflation, is exactly the tension Kevin Warsh has to address on Friday.

JENNY: Which makes his speech even harder to read ahead of time.

ANDREW: That's the view from Washington and Tehran. Jenny, what's happening back home in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a hot, stormy one today — a high near ninety-three, with an 80 percent chance of afternoon thunderstorms and lows in the mid-seventies tonight.

JENNY: Closer to home, the Jacksonville Transportation Authority's board meets today and is expected to name an interim CEO — the first concrete step in replacing Nat Ford, who's leaving for Dallas Area Rapid Transit this fall.

ANDREW: Remind me — why is Ford leaving, and who's actually in the running?

JENNY: He was named to lead Dallas's transit agency back on July 21st and starts there October 26th. As for who's next, the JTA board has been clear from the start that it wants to keep this internal — no outside names being considered for the interim role — so today's pick will be a sitting agency executive stepping up while a national search firm looks for a permanent successor. And the backdrop matters here: JTA is also sitting on a projected thirty-one point eight million dollar deficit for this fiscal year, so whoever steps in inherits a real budget problem on day one.

JENNY: Also today, the city council's finance committee is back at it, a full day of budget hearings at City Hall as members work through Mayor Deegan's roughly two billion dollar spending plan. Chair Will Lahnen has been pushing a preserve-cash message all month, largely because of what's on the ballot in November — a proposed increase to the homestead exemption that city auditors estimate could cost Jacksonville more than three hundred million dollars a year in lost revenue by 2029. This is one of several hearings the committee has scheduled this week alone, as members try to lock in savings now in case that ballot measure passes in November.

ANDREW: That's a lot of budget planning happening under a pretty big question mark.

JENNY: It really is. And Jaguars fans headed to EverBank Stadium this season should brace for a construction zone. The team's one point four billion dollar Stadium of the Future project is underway, and capacity is down to about forty-two thousand seats this year, roughly 62 percent of normal, while crews install the steel trusses for a new canopy roof. The stadium is expected to grow to around seventy thousand seats once the project wraps in 2028.

JENNY: And in a smaller but very Jacksonville story this morning, News4Jax is reporting that an abandoned sailboat has been anchored for weeks in the exact spot a sixty-year-old marine towing company needs to move its equipment on the river, effectively freezing part of that family business's operations until the boat gets cleared out.

ANDREW: Sixty years in business, stopped cold by one abandoned boat.

JENNY: Andrew, speaking of big numbers, what's happening on the mortgage side this week?

ANDREW: Rates are holding fairly steady in that high-six range we mentioned earlier, and the Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey shows demand basically flat — applications down about half a percent for the week, with purchase activity down two percent and refinancing still running around 18 percent below year-ago levels, even though it ticked up slightly week to week.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for someone trying to buy a house right now?

ANDREW: Nationally, it means demand stays soft as long as rates sit above six and a half percent. But here in Jacksonville specifically, it's actually a fairly balanced market — local listing data has the median sale price around three hundred ten thousand dollars, with roughly four months of inventory on hand. That's enough supply that buyers have real room to negotiate, which isn't true everywhere in the country right now. New listings are also moving at a reasonable clip, spending about a month on market on average, so it's a healthier local picture than the national headlines about soft demand might suggest.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's own agenda points to a final rule on mortgage servicing landing as soon as this month, part of a broader push under an executive order aimed at cutting compliance costs for lenders. And the Federal Housing Finance Agency has pulled back an earlier directive telling Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to police unfair lending practices themselves, with FHFA's director arguing that enforcement belongs with the Federal Trade Commission, not the mortgage giants. Regulators also quietly raised the dollar threshold that triggers extra appraisal requirements on higher-priced loans, from thirty-three thousand five hundred dollars to thirty-four thousand two hundred, a small but real easing on paperwork costs for some borrowers and lenders.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for what's happening in AI and tech.

JENNY: Anthropic's roughly six to seven billion dollar deal to acquire the Israeli AI infrastructure startup Decart still hasn't been signed. The two sides are reportedly trading advanced drafts, with a signing possible as soon as next month.

ANDREW: What does Decart actually do that's worth that kind of money?

JENNY: They build software that helps AI chips run more efficiently, cutting the cost of training and operating large models. For a company burning through enormous amounts of compute, that's a strategic buy aimed at controlling costs, not just picking up talent. It's also notable timing, because Anthropic is separately gearing up for an IPO — it confidentially filed paperwork with the SEC back in June, and reports suggest the public filing could come within days, targeting a Nasdaq listing this fall. That confidential filing came just weeks after Anthropic closed a sixty-five billion dollar funding round that valued the company at nearly a trillion dollars, so whenever this IPO actually lands, it's shaping up to be one of the largest in history.

JENNY: And tonight is the big one for the whole AI trade. Nvidia reports its fiscal second-quarter results after the closing bell. Wall Street is looking for revenue of about ninety-two billion dollars, which would be up roughly 97 percent from a year ago. However this print lands, it tends to set the tone for tech stocks for days afterward.

ANDREW: We'll have the numbers for you tomorrow morning either way.

JENNY: Fair, though if history is any guide, the stock's reaction over the following days tends to matter more than the headline number itself.

JENNY: One more data point on how AI is actually landing inside big companies. Protiviti's latest global finance survey found the share of finance teams using AI for forecasting jumped from 58 percent to 76 percent over the past year. But only about a third of those organizations say they can actually measure whether that investment is paying off, and security and data privacy remain finance leaders' top concern heading into next year, even as AI budgets keep climbing. Adoption is outrunning proof that it works.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday morning at 10 AM Eastern, with markets currently pricing in roughly one-in-three odds of a rate move at next month's Fed meeting. Watch whether he leans toward inflation-fighting language or signals any openness to cutting. His tone in that speech could move Treasury yields, and mortgage rates, more than anything else happening this week.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you right back here tomorrow morning.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Tanker Hit Near Hormuz, Warsh's Jackson Hole Test, JTA Picks a Chief
item.description: A tanker is disabled near the Strait of Hormuz hours after Treasury's new Iran sanctions, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh faces his first Jackson Hole speech, Jacksonville's transit board picks a leader, and Nvidia's price hikes rattle chip stocks.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, August 25th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Overnight, an unidentified projectile disabled an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, just hours after Treasury unveiled its toughest sanctions yet against Iran. We'll get into what that means for oil and for markets.

ANDREW: And chip stocks took a hit yesterday after Bloomberg reported Nvidia is raising AI server prices by more than 15 percent. We'll dig into why.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 slipped about three tenths of a percent to close at 7,652. The Dow bucked the trend, adding around 140 points, roughly a quarter percent, to finish at 53,417. The Nasdaq lagged behind, down about eight tenths of a percent to 25,980, dragged lower by chip stocks. The ten-year Treasury yield sits around four point seven percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the high sixes, according to Mortgage News Daily. Oil actually fell yesterday, with U.S. crude down about two and a half percent to just under 85 dollars a barrel, as traders took profits. That was before overnight news of a tanker attack near Hormuz, so watch how oil opens this morning.

ANDREW: Let's start with that story, because it's moving fastest. A vessel was struck by an unknown projectile Monday night a few miles off the coast of Oman, disabling its engine. The UK Maritime Trade Organization confirmed the crew is safe, and there's been no claim of responsibility.

JENNY: Does this connect to the sanctions news from yesterday?

ANDREW: It's the backdrop, if not necessarily the direct cause. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled what he's calling Operation Economic Outcast on Monday, sanctioning nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels tied to Iran's oil, shipping, gold, and crypto networks. He's calling it a warning shot, holding off on the harshest secondary sanctions for now, but making clear any country still doing business with Tehran, China included, is on notice. Iran's currency hit a record low within hours, more than two million rials to the dollar.

JENNY: So is this tanker strike Iran's response?

ANDREW: Nobody's claiming it yet, and it's worth noting Iran has periodically fired on or harassed vessels near the strait for months now without formally claiming those incidents. But it lands exactly where Iran's security chief threatened to strike back if Gulf states and global banks fall in line behind Washington's pressure campaign. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil still moves through that strait every day, even with traffic well below pre-war levels, so any pattern of attacks there is the kind of thing that can move oil prices fast.

JENNY: Remind me, how long has this war actually been going on now?

ANDREW: Nearly six months, since late February. The Pentagon says at least 18 U.S. service members have died since it began, and this latest sanctions push, plus overnight's tanker strike, is a sign it's still escalating rather than winding down. For context, the last time Hormuz saw sustained attacks like this was during the so-called tanker war of the 1980s, and that eventually pulled the U.S. Navy into direct escort duty. Nobody's suggesting we're there yet, but that's the kind of historical marker analysts are watching for.

ANDREW: There's also a domestic thread tying into all of this. Kevin Warsh, who's now been Fed chair for about three months, delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote this Friday morning, and Wall Street is watching closely. The symposium in Wyoming runs Thursday through Saturday, and Warsh speaks at ten a.m. Eastern on Friday.

JENNY: What's everyone listening for?

ANDREW: Any signal on where he leans heading into the Fed's September 15th and 16th meeting. Treasury yields have been volatile for weeks, mortgage rates have followed, and this is Warsh's first big public moment to frame how he sees that volatility, and inflation, which is still running above the Fed's target. If he sounds more dovish than markets expect, look for yields, and eventually mortgage rates, to ease. If he sounds cautious, expect the opposite.

ANDREW: Two quick updates on stories we've been tracking. On the White House ballroom fight, Chief Justice Roberts's stay from Friday remains in place, construction is continuing, and the administration still hasn't had its formal stay petition resolved by the full Court, so that underlying question of who controls spending on federal property is still unsettled. And in Indiana, power crews have restored all but a small fraction of the customers knocked out by that flooding two weeks ago, with full restoration expected any day now, though the White House still hasn't acted on the state's request for a major disaster declaration covering fifty-four counties.

ANDREW: Jenny, closer to home.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 90 degrees today, with a good chance of afternoon thunderstorms, so keep an eye on the sky if you've got outdoor plans.

JENNY: The story we've been following all week is JTA's leadership search. The board is expected to name an interim CEO from inside the agency at a board meeting this week, as it works to replace Nat Ford, who's leaving for a transit job in Dallas. As of this morning, no decision has been announced.

ANDREW: Whoever gets that job is walking into a financial mess, right? The deficit numbers we talked about yesterday.

JENNY: Exactly, nearly 32 million dollars projected for this year, up from just over 2 million six months ago. That's the backdrop for whoever steps in, even on an interim basis.

JENNY: Meanwhile, City Council's Finance Committee is back at it Wednesday and Thursday, grinding through Mayor Deegan's roughly 2 billion dollar budget for next year. Chair Will Lahnen's message hasn't changed: preserve cash, because a November ballot measure that would sharply raise the homestead exemption could cost the city more than 300 million dollars a year in lost tax revenue within a few years if it passes.

ANDREW: Any other local business news?

JENNY: Yes, and it's a real milestone for JEA. Florida regulators approved the utility's request to build a new 675-megawatt natural gas plant on Jacksonville's Northside, a project worth about one and a half billion dollars. It'll rise on the old St. Johns River Power Park site, where JEA shut down a coal plant back in 2018, and it's meant to come online in 2031 to keep up with growth across Northeast Florida.

ANDREW: That's a long runway for a project that size.

JENNY: It is, but JEA's argument is that Northeast Florida's population growth doesn't wait, and they need to start now to have power ready by the early 2030s. And speaking of long construction timelines, the Jaguars are still playing this entire season inside one, with capacity down to about 42,500 seats while crews build around the fans on that 1.4 billion dollar Stadium of the Future renovation. The team already has NFL approval to play next season, 2027, at Camping World Stadium in Orlando while the heaviest construction wraps up here, with the goal of moving back home for good in 2028.

ANDREW: A two-year road trip for a home team.

JENNY: Pretty much, but city and team officials are treating it as the cost of getting a modern stadium built without shutting football down completely. Andrew, speaking of things that take years to build, what's happening with mortgage rates given all this yield volatility you mentioned?

ANDREW: It's a mixed bag, but trending slightly better than a couple weeks ago. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the thirty-year fixed at six point six five percent last week, its second straight weekly decline. Daily trackers like Mortgage News Daily and Zillow have it in a similar range, high sixes, occasionally dipping just under six point seven.

JENNY: Does that mean it's actually a better time to buy?

ANDREW: A little better, but buyers are still cautious. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey showed purchase applications down about 2 percent from the week before, and refinance activity, while it ticked up slightly week over week, is still down nearly a fifth from a year ago. For context, a year ago at this time the thirty-year fixed was averaging six point five eight percent, according to Freddie Mac, so today's rate isn't actually that far off where it stood twelve months back, even after all this volatility. People are watching the same thing we are, whether yields settle down, and Friday's Warsh speech could be the next real catalyst either way.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau could finalize a new mortgage servicing rule as soon as this month, aimed at cutting compliance costs tied to how lenders handle borrowers who fall behind on payments. It's part of a broader push to loosen some of the paperwork burden on lenders without touching consumer protections. The bureau also just wrapped up a public comment period on a separate proposal to ease disclosure requirements more broadly, so there's a real chance we see more than one rule change land before the year's out.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you for tech, because that chip selloff we mentioned at the top ties into your beat.

JENNY: It does. Nvidia is raising prices on servers built around its newest AI chips by more than 15 percent, according to Bloomberg. Microsoft, Google, and Oracle have all reportedly been notified, and that's what dragged the Nasdaq down yesterday, with Micron losing nearly 6 percent.

ANDREW: Wait, 15 percent? Why now?

JENNY: The driver is memory chip costs, they've been climbing sharply, and memory is a core, expensive component in these AI server systems. The price hikes apply to servers built around Nvidia's newest Vera Rubin and Blackwell chip lines, shipping early next year. It's a reminder that even as AI spending keeps climbing, the hardware underneath it isn't getting any cheaper, and that cost eventually flows through to whoever's renting that compute.

ANDREW: That connects to Anthropic, doesn't it? They're one of the biggest buyers of exactly that kind of compute.

JENNY: Right, and Anthropic's got two things still in motion. That roughly 6 to 7 billion dollar acquisition of Decart, the Israeli AI infrastructure startup, still hasn't been signed as of this morning, even though reports describe the two sides as trading advanced drafts. And Anthropic's IPO is still on track for a Nasdaq listing this fall, with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan leading it, though there's no public filing date yet. All of this is happening against the backdrop of a company whose annualized revenue run rate hit 65 billion dollars at the end of July, more than it made in all of last year combined, which is exactly why hardware costs like Nvidia's price hikes matter so much to their bottom line.

ANDREW: A lot of moving pieces there. Worth watching whether that Decart deal actually closes.

JENNY: Definitely, that's one we'll keep tracking.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Friday morning, when Fed Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote at ten a.m. Eastern. It's his first major public test since taking over in May, and with Treasury yields elevated and mortgage rates stuck in the high sixes, markets will be parsing every word for a signal on the Fed's September 15th meeting. Watch oil too, given that tanker strike near Hormuz overnight. If Iran or its proxies escalate further, that's the kind of shock that ripples fast into gas prices, inflation, and everything the Fed is trying to manage.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Sanctions Blitz, JTA's Deficit Triples, Claude Designs Proteins
item.description: Treasury unveils a sweeping sanctions campaign against Iran as Tehran threatens the Strait of Hormuz, Jacksonville's transit agency reveals a deficit nearly tripling, and Anthropic's Claude designs working proteins in a lab.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, August 24th, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this morning unveiled what he's calling the most aggressive sanctions campaign yet against Iran, aimed, in his words, at collapsing the regime. Tehran is already threatening to seize ships and choke off traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in response.

ANDREW: And closer to home, a new city audit shows Jacksonville's transit agency saw its budget deficit nearly triple in a single quarter. We'll get into what that means for the search for a new CEO there.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. Since it's Monday, we're working off Friday's close. The S and P 500 finished at 7,674, up about four tenths of a percent. The Dow jumped roughly 518 points, a full percent, to close at 53,277. The Nasdaq added about four tenths of a percent, closing at 26,180. But zoom out to the full week and all three indexes were actually down, as bond market turmoil overshadowed some strong earnings — the S and P lost one point four percent, the Dow eight tenths of a percent, and the Nasdaq a full two percent. The ten-year Treasury yield sits around four point seven percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the high sixes, according to Mortgage News Daily. We'll dig into that in a few minutes.

ANDREW: If you were off the grid this weekend, here's the headline version. The Supreme Court's chief justice cleared the way Friday night for construction to resume on the White House ballroom project. Treasury rolled out that new Iran sanctions campaign this morning. And Anthropic says its Claude models designed working proteins in a lab for the first time. Let's start with Iran, because that story is moving the fastest.

ANDREW: Bessent's new sanctions target Iran's oil-smuggling networks, its banks, its ship registries, and shell companies used to move money. But the real teeth are aimed outward — he says any nation or bank still doing business with Tehran, and that includes the Chinese refineries that buy the vast majority of Iran's oil exports, should expect to be isolated right along with it.

JENNY: That's striking language for a Treasury official. How is Iran responding?

ANDREW: Not well. Iran's security chief is threatening to start seizing ships and potentially shut down oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz if Gulf neighbors line up behind this pressure campaign. That's not an empty threat — roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through that strait. And this war is nearly six months old now. The UAE already cut off trade with Iran back on August 19th after accusing Tehran of firing near its shipping, and separate talks between Iran and Oman over safe transit through Hormuz just hit a snag, with Oman's foreign minister reportedly saying this week that his country doesn't actually support the transit fees Iran's been pushing for.

JENNY: So even the diplomatic track is stalling. What does all of this do to oil prices?

ANDREW: That's the number to watch. Any actual disruption at Hormuz would send crude prices sharply higher almost overnight, since so much of the world's supply funnels through that one waterway. Markets haven't fully priced that in yet, because traders have heard threats like this before without a follow-through. But the sanctions announcement today is a real escalation, not just rhetoric, and it raises the odds that someone overreacts. The Pentagon, meanwhile, says at least eighteen US service members have died since the war began in February, so this is very much a live, escalating situation, not one that's cooling off.

ANDREW: Meanwhile, the Supreme Court intervened Friday night in that fight over White House ballroom construction. Chief Justice Roberts issued a stay clearing the way for builders to keep working on the roughly 400 million dollar project, overriding a lower court ruling that only Congress can authorize spending like that on federal property.

JENNY: Does that settle the underlying legal question?

ANDREW: No, it doesn't. Roberts acted alone, not the full Court, and there's no expiration date on the stay. The government still has to file a formal petition, and the justices could revisit it. So construction resumes for now, but the constitutional question of who controls spending on federal property is still very much unresolved.

ANDREW: And that Treasury yield mention from the markets segment ties into a bigger story. The thirty-year Treasury yield hit five point three three percent last week, the highest level since 2007, before easing back to around five point two percent after Bessent doubled the size of the government's long-bond buybacks. He's called that four billion dollar figure a floor, not a ceiling, meaning he's ready to do more if yields keep climbing. The Fed's next meeting is September 15th and 16th, and this bond market turbulence is exactly the kind of backdrop that could shape what they decide.

JENNY: A lot riding on that meeting, then.

ANDREW: A lot riding on it. Markets have been assuming the Fed leans toward cutting rates this fall, but a bond market this jumpy makes that harder to call with confidence. We haven't seen individual Fed officials stake out clear positions on the record yet, so watch for that in the next few weeks as the meeting gets closer.

ANDREW: One more update, and this one's hopeful. That flooding in Indiana that killed seven people and knocked out power to more than 360,000 customers at its peak — utility crews say northwest Indiana should be back to full power by tomorrow night, down from tens of thousands of households still dark just a few days ago. The open question now is whether the White House approves the state's request for a full disaster declaration covering more than fifty counties, which would unlock more federal aid beyond the smaller emergency declaration already in place. That's still pending.

ANDREW: Jenny, closer to home, Jacksonville had its own busy weekend.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 96 degrees today, with a heat index around 105 and a decent chance of strong storms rolling through this evening, so plan around that commute home.

JENNY: The big local story right now is our transit agency, JTA. A new city audit released last week shows their projected deficit for this year has ballooned to nearly 32 million dollars, up from just two and a quarter million dollars projected only six months earlier.

ANDREW: Wait, it grew that much in one quarter?

JENNY: That's right, almost 30 million dollars worse in about three months. Roughly 17 million of that comes from sales and gas tax collections coming in weaker than expected. But auditors also flagged that JTA owes more than 15 million dollars in unpaid bills, some dating back to 2014, with one vendor alone owed nearly three and a half million. A city finance committee member didn't mince words, calling it, quote, red flags of a failing business.

ANDREW: That's a rough backdrop for a leadership transition.

JENNY: Exactly, and that's the timing problem. JTA still hasn't named an interim CEO since Nat Ford left for a transit job in Dallas. The board is expected to pick someone from inside the agency at Thursday's meeting, so whoever gets that job walks straight into this financial mess.

JENNY: Separately, City Council is deep into budget hearings for next year, and Finance Committee Chair Will Lahnen has been blunt about the mood, saying this is, quote, the year to preserve cash. Part of the worry is a statewide ballot measure in November, Amendment 3, that would roughly triple Florida's homestead exemption. If it passes, city auditors estimate Jacksonville could lose more than 300 million dollars a year in tax revenue by 2029.

ANDREW: Any good news on that front?

JENNY: A little. A coalition of local funders, including Northern Trust and the Jessie Ball duPont Fund, just launched a 20 million dollar affordable housing loan fund they're calling the Jax GAP Fund, aiming to leverage that into about 80 million dollars of new affordable housing across the city.

JENNY: And down at the stadium, the Jaguars just got city approval for a new sales center previewing their 1.4 billion dollar Stadium of the Future renovation, a reminder that the team is playing this entire season inside an active construction zone that won't wrap up until 2028. Capacity is down to about 42,500 seats this year, roughly sixty percent of normal, while crews build around the fans.

ANDREW: A construction zone during football season sounds like a logistical headache.

JENNY: It is, but city and team officials seem to think it's worth it for what comes after. The mayor's office is treating it as the anchor of the whole downtown push, alongside things like that new housing fund we just talked about.

JENNY: Andrew, back to your beat. What's happening with mortgage rates?

ANDREW: Honestly, it's a bit of a confusing picture right now. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the thirty-year fixed at six point six five percent last week, its second straight weekly decline. But Mortgage News Daily's daily rate, which reacts faster to the bond market, has it closer to six point seven seven percent, and other trackers put it anywhere from six point six to six point eight.

JENNY: So which number should someone actually trust if they're shopping for a rate this week?

ANDREW: Think of it as a range in the high sixes rather than one hard number, where you land depends on your lender, your credit, and exactly which day you lock. The bigger driver is that Treasury yield volatility we talked about earlier. When yields spike the way they did last week, mortgage rates tend to follow with a lag, and that relief rally from the Treasury's bond buybacks hasn't really held.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is expected to issue a new mortgage servicing rule as soon as this month, aimed at cutting compliance costs for lenders. It's part of a broader push from the White House to make it cheaper and easier for lenders to originate and service loans.

JENNY: Is that actually translating into more people buying homes?

ANDREW: Not yet. The Mortgage Bankers Association says purchase applications are down about three percent from a year ago, and refinance activity is down nearly a fifth. That tells you rate-sensitive buyers are still largely sitting on the sidelines, waiting for something to give, whether that's rates easing or just more clarity on where the economy is headed. The one bright spot is on the lender side, where industry surveys show loan profitability has actually been improving this year, even with volume soft.

ANDREW: Jenny, on a completely different note, I hear there was some notable AI news this weekend.

JENNY: There was, and it's a genuinely interesting one. Anthropic says its Claude models designed functional proteins in a lab setting for the first time. Not just predictions on a screen, actual working molecules.

ANDREW: How do you even verify something like that?

JENNY: Independent labs built them. Claude was given fifteen drug-relevant targets tied to things like cancer and inflammation, and it designed more than 1,300 candidate proteins. Two outside partners, Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, manufactured and tested them on the bench, and confirmed working binders for fourteen of the fifteen targets, with hit rates roughly double the industry average.

ANDREW: That's a real result, not just a demo.

JENNY: Right, and it's a good example of AI moving from writing code to doing actual scientific legwork. In a related test, Anthropic says a newer model processed lab spectral data, the kind chemists use to check a compound's purity, in under 25 minutes, and its readout matched the lab's own results almost exactly.

ANDREW: So the model isn't just designing the molecule, it's helping check the work too.

JENNY: Exactly, and that combination, design plus verification, is what's got people in the life sciences paying attention. Meanwhile, Anthropic's business side keeps accelerating. Their annualized revenue run rate hit 65 billion dollars at the end of July, more than the entire company made in all of last year combined.

ANDREW: That's a staggering growth curve for a company that's only a few years old.

JENNY: It is, and it's why the IPO talk keeps getting louder. Anthropic's still targeting a listing sometime this fall, with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan lined up to lead it. A separate deal is also in the works, a roughly six to seven billion dollar acquisition of an Israeli AI startup called Decart, mostly in Anthropic stock. Reports describe it as close, but as of this morning, it still isn't signed.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week. Thursday, when Jacksonville's transit board is expected to name a new interim CEO for JTA, and separately, whether the White House approves Indiana's disaster declaration request. But the bigger one to watch is whether Treasury's new sanctions campaign actually gets Gulf allies and countries like China to fall in line, or whether Tehran follows through on its threat to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. That's the kind of shock that could ripple straight into oil prices, and from there, into markets and mortgage rates alike.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Treasury Yields Spike, Stocks Slide, SCOTUS Ballroom Deadline Today
item.description: Markets post their worst day since late July as Treasury yields whipsaw, the Supreme Court faces a same-day deadline on the White House ballroom pause, and Anthropic's revenue run rate hits 65 billion dollars ahead of a fall IPO.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, August 21st. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Wall Street just had its worst day since late July, the Supreme Court is facing a deadline today in the fight over building a ballroom at the White House, and the United Arab Emirates has now cut trade ties with Iran entirely.

ANDREW: And on the tech side, Anthropic just told investors its revenue run rate has hit 65 billion dollars as it barrels toward a fall IPO. We'll get into what that means for the AI race.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,641, down about 9 tenths of a percent. The Dow fell more than 700 points, off about 1.3 percent, its worst session since July 29th. The Nasdaq dropped roughly 1 percent to just over 26,000. It was a rough session all around. A Treasury plan meant to hold down long-term interest rates lost its punch, Walmart shares sank more than 9 percent after weak sales numbers, and rising oil prices tied to the Iran standoff didn't help. The ten-year Treasury yield sits just above 4.7 percent, and the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking in the mid-6 percent range. More on that in a few minutes.

ANDREW: The through-line today is bond yields. Every one of those stories, the stock selloff, the mortgage rate whiplash, even some of the pressure on the federal budget, traces back to how expensive it's gotten for the government to borrow money over the long term.

ANDREW: Let's start in Washington, because there's a deadline today that's been building all week.

ANDREW: A federal appeals court ruled the administration doesn't have the unilateral authority to build a 90,000 square foot ballroom at the White House without money appropriated by Congress. That court's construction pause is set to take effect today unless the Supreme Court steps in first. The administration's solicitor general has asked the justices for an emergency stay, and as of this morning, they haven't ruled.

JENNY: So what actually happens at the construction site if the Court just doesn't act today?

ANDREW: Then the pause kicks in automatically and work stops until there's a ruling on the merits. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the case, wants that pause to hold. The administration argues halting construction mid-project is itself a security risk. We could know more within hours.

JENNY: This has been your one thing to watch two mornings running. Why is it taking this long to resolve?
