ANDREW: Because the underlying legal question is bigger than one building. It's about whether a White House can spend on major construction without Congress appropriating the money first. However the justices come down, it'll set a precedent well beyond this one ballroom.

ANDREW: Meanwhile, the Iran standoff keeps widening. It's been nearly six months since the war began in late February, and this week the President announced a new sanctions campaign, calling it Economic D-Day, aimed at the networks that help Iran move oil, cash, and ships around the blockade. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has floated secondary sanctions on any country or company still doing business with Tehran, though the administration hasn't published an actual target list yet.

JENNY: And the Emirates pulling out, that's new since yesterday, right?

ANDREW: It is. The U.A.E. announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran after accusing Tehran of firing two ballistic missiles into its waters. Iran denies that and calls it a false flag. It matters because the Emirates has been one of Iran's largest trading partners, supplying something like a third of its imports, so losing that access tightens the squeeze considerably. Separately, Oman is still trying to broker an arrangement with Iran over safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Both sides say they're close, but there's no deal yet.

JENNY: Six months in, is there any sense of how much longer this goes?

ANDREW: No clear end point yet. The Pentagon has confirmed at least 18 American service members killed since the war began in February, and the White House is clearly betting that economic pressure, rather than a bigger military push, is what finally forces a resolution. That's the whole logic behind this sanctions campaign.

ANDREW: One more to flag out of Indiana. The death toll from this month's flooding is holding at seven, but recovery is getting harder before it gets easier. The Wabash River crested at roughly 25 feet at Terre Haute yesterday, major flood stage, and in the northwest part of the state, tens of thousands of households are now in their ninth day without power, with utilities not expecting full restoration until the middle of next week. A full federal disaster declaration is still working through review.

JENNY: Nine days without power in August. That's brutal.

ANDREW: It is, and it's part of why that declaration matters. It unlocks the federal money for things like generators and cooling centers. The President already approved a smaller emergency declaration covering 53 counties on August 15th. This next one, the major disaster declaration, is what actually pays for rebuilding.

JENNY: Sticking with money for a second. Andrew, what's going on with mortgage rates this week?

ANDREW: It's actually a split story. Freddie Mac's weekly survey has the 30 year fixed averaging 6.65 percent, the second straight weekly decline. But Mortgage News Daily's faster-moving daily tracker showed rates popping back up to 6.76 percent yesterday, the highest in about a week.

JENNY: So which number do I trust if I'm trying to lock a rate right now?

ANDREW: Watch the daily number. It reacts faster to what's happening in the bond market, and this has been a volatile week. Long-term Treasury yields spiked as high as 5.33 percent earlier this week, the highest since the 2007, 2008 crisis. That prompted Secretary Bessent to announce the government is doubling its long-bond buybacks to try to calm things down. It worked for about a day, then yesterday's selloff gave some of that back.

ANDREW: There's a slower-moving story underneath all of this too. HousingWire reports FHA loan delinquencies climbed to just over 2 percent in the second quarter, up nearly half a point from a year ago, with delinquencies on Veterans Affairs backed loans rising as well, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data. The stress is concentrated among borrowers with lower credit scores and higher debt loads. It's a reminder that even as headline rates ease a little, plenty of borrowers are still under real strain.

JENNY: So the affordability squeeze isn't over just because rates ticked down.

ANDREW: Not even close. And remember, this time last year the 30 year fixed was closer to 6 and a quarter percent. A lot of would-be buyers who were priced out then are still priced out now, even with the recent easing.

ANDREW: That's it from the money desk. Jenny, over to you. What's happening in AI?

JENNY: Big number out of Anthropic this week. The company told investors its annualized revenue run rate hit 65 billion dollars by the end of July. That's up from 47 billion in May, and something like 9 billion at the end of last year. For context, that's a company most people had never heard of five years ago now running at a scale that rivals some Fortune 500 giants.

ANDREW: Wait, that's more than a six-fold jump in seven months?

JENNY: Basically, yes. Second quarter revenue alone topped 11 and a half billion dollars, compared to under a billion a year earlier. The company is now projecting revenue as high as 200 billion dollars by 2028. All of this is landing as Anthropic prepares for an IPO expected sometime in September or October, with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan leading the offering.

JENNY: One deal still hasn't closed, though. Anthropic's reported six to seven billion dollar acquisition of the video AI startup Decart remains unsigned as of this week, even though it's been described as close for several days now. We'll keep watching for when, or if, that actually gets announced.

JENNY: And in a separate deal that shows how much money is flowing into AI infrastructure, Google gave the chipmaker Marvell warrants worth up to 12 billion dollars, tied to Google's custom AI chip purchases through 2033. Marvell's stock jumped about 10 percent on the news. Shares of Broadcom, which had been Google's main chip partner, fell more than 5 percent.

ANDREW: That's a real shift in the pecking order.

JENNY: It is, and it shows just how much the major tech players think they'll need in custom silicon over the next decade. Put it together with Anthropic's numbers, and you've got two signals pointing the same direction: the money moving into AI infrastructure and enterprise adoption isn't slowing down, it's compounding.

JENNY: Let's bring it home to Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 96 today, with scattered afternoon storms and a heat advisory in effect from 11 this morning until 7 tonight.

JENNY: On the budget front, the city's Finance Committee wrapped its third hearing of the week yesterday, still trying to build a cash cushion ahead of November's Amendment 3 vote, the property tax measure that could cost the city upward of 150 million dollars next year, climbing past 300 million a year after that.

ANDREW: Remind me what that measure actually does?

JENNY: It expands the homestead exemption, which is good news for individual homeowners' tax bills, but it shrinks the tax base the city budgets around. That's why the Council is trying to bank cash now. Finance Chair Will Lahnen has been blunt about it, calling this the year to preserve cash rather than spend it. Also yesterday, a group of private funders, including Northern Trust, the Jessie Ball duPont Fund, the Community Foundation for Northeast Florida, and Pinnacle Financial Partners, announced a new 20 million dollar fund to make low-cost loans available to affordable housing developers here, separate from the city's own budget fight.

ANDREW: Good timing, given everything else you just described.

JENNY: That's exactly why it's notable. Private money stepping in for affordable housing right as the city's own trust fund for that same purpose is getting trimmed.

JENNY: Over at JTA, the transit authority, the board is still on track to name an interim CEO as soon as next week, choosing from internal candidates only, as outgoing CEO Nat Ford heads to Dallas this fall. New context from the Jax Daily Record this week: the agency is facing a revenue shortfall of roughly 17 million dollars, driven mostly by lower than expected sales and gas tax collections, so whoever steps in inherits a tight balance sheet.

JENNY: And Jacksonville's utility, JEA, cleared a state hurdle this week. Florida regulators approved the need for JEA's planned 1.6 billion dollar natural gas plant at the old St. Johns River Power Park site, keeping it on track for a 2031 start date.

ANDREW: That's a big build for JEA.

JENNY: It is, their biggest generation project in years. The plant would replace aging capacity at that same site and is meant to keep pace with growth here in Northeast Florida over the next decade.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch today: whether the Supreme Court rules on the White House ballroom construction pause before the day is out. The lower court's injunction takes effect today by default, so silence from the Court effectively means construction stops. Watch for an emergency order, likely this afternoon.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you Monday.

JENNY: Have a good weekend.
